Summary: The paper proposes CertGate, a selective-prediction gate for multi-site clinical risk models that certifies, with confidence 1-delta, that an influence-weighted answered-set error rate (R_M) averaged over the population of sites stays at or below a budget alpha, treating the site (hospital) rather than the record as the unit of statistical independence. Each calibration site is collapsed to a bounded atom Z_c (influence cap M=100), a Waudby-Smith-Ramdas betting martingale tests the site-mean against alpha, and a fixed-sequence (learn-then-test style) walk over a 23-point threshold grid, ordered on a disjoint auxiliary split, selects the operating threshold without delta-splitting; two rungs alpha in {0.05, 0.10} are combined at 1-2delta. Two assumption modes are shipped and named in the guarantee text: an exchangeable baseline and a BBSE label-shift mode whose four estimated parameters carry a Bonferroni-split cluster-bootstrap/Clopper-Pearson uncertainty box tested at both odds-ratio endpoints; concept shift is explicitly out of scope. An L2-logistic head yields exact additive attributions for answers and abstentions, and a three-way answered-set composition disclosure accompanies every certificate. Validation comprises a 208-site synthetic grid (E1 validity, E2 label shift, E3 verified-falsifiable concept-shift control, E4 site-count frontier, E5 explanations, E6 per-site coverage/composition, E7 record-as-unit comparator, plus an M-sensitivity sweep) and an eICU-CRD v2.0 study (164,322 stays, 207 hospitals) under a protocol frozen before the extract was read. Headline results: alpha=0.10 certifies on all synthetic draws (0.98 coverage, zero aggregate exceedances) and on 20/20 eICU by-site re-splits (0.890 coverage); alpha=0.05 certifies nothing at this site count and needs ~300-400 sites; the uncorrected baseline certifies-and-violates 39.5% under prevalence shift while BBSE declines all draws; the concept-shift control fails as excluded; the record-as-unit comparator violates its aggregate budget at 3.5%/9.6% under two heterogeneity levels; and on eICU the answered set's mortality (0.046) is about half the pool's (0.090).
Strengths: All five reviewers agree the problem is real and under-served: record-level selective-risk certificates are silently overconfident under site-clustered clinical deployment, and making the site the atom of a finite-sample certificate is the correct first-order fix, aligned with TRIPOD-Cluster / internal-external validation practice.

The exchangeable-mode certification core is technically sound as far as reviewers could verify: bounded per-site atoms with E[Z] <= alpha iff R_M <= alpha, a capped predictable bet keeping the wealth process a nonnegative supermartingale under H0, Ville's inequality for the delta level, threshold ordering computed on a disjoint auxiliary split so the fixed-sequence walk spends no extra confidence, and Bonferroni combination over the alpha ladder. The demonstration that naive truncation of realized contributions is anti-conservative is a nice touch.

The guarantee text is unusually careful and candid: it names what is not bounded (per-site risk, realized counts, concept shift), states the site-population-average estimand precisely, and travels with dispersion, composition and always-negative-comparison disclosures. Reviewers uniformly credited the authors' honesty about the gate's cost (answered-set mortality half the pool's, negative answered-minus-all skill contrast, one hospital at 0.29 answered error under a valid certificate).

The validation harness is more careful than most: an oracle synthetic generator, a negative control verified capable of failing before it is used (E3), a record-as-unit comparator run on identical draws (E7), a sensitivity sweep of the one influential constant (M from 25 to 5000), and a real-data study with cohort predicates, feature allowlist, leak denylist, seven predictions and five failure criteria committed before the extract was read; falsified predictions are reported as falsified and a leak screen that fired in the unexpected direction is documented. An external clinical comparator (APACHE-IVa) is reported on the answered set.

Reproducibility is strong: released code, a single protocol seed, constants pinned by unit tests, byte-identical regeneration of the synthetic grid, and an aggregate-only release policy consistent with the PhysioNet DUA. The site-count frontier and M sweep provide useful capacity-planning information.
Weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited for a prestigious ML venue (unanimous). The certificate is a direct composition of existing tools: WSR betting for bounded means, cluster-as-unit atoms (Dunn et al.; Lee et al.), fixed-sequence LTT threshold selection, BBSE, and the uncertainty-in-the-guarantee pattern of Si et al. The influence weight g_c = min(n_c, M) and the atom linearization are minor; the 'exact attributions' are coefficient x centered feature for a logistic head; the authors themselves concede that contributions 3 and 4 are supporting practice rather than independent methods. The delta over prior work is engineering and disclosure discipline rather than a new statistical idea.

The only certifiable rung is close to trivial at the working prevalence (unanimous, and the most damaging point). At ~9% prevalence with a symmetric 0-1 loss, an always-negative rule already meets alpha=0.10 (0.1039 error on synthetic pools; 0.089 on eICU); the eICU answered set has 0.046 mortality, answered error 0.042, and the post-hoc panel's skill margin over the constant rule is 0.0039 with a negative answered-minus-all contrast. The budget is met partly by abstaining where deaths concentrate. The rung that would be clinically meaningful (alpha=0.05) is unreachable at every tested scale and every M, needing ~300-400 hospitals. The paper discloses this, but disclosure does not restore practical significance to the headline '20/20 certified' result.

The label-shift mode (contribution 2) is evidenced only by refusal. It declines 200/200 draws at every non-null shift, certifies 9% at the null point (vs 100% for the baseline), and returns failsafe on eICU (rho-hat 0.668, box [0.068, 1.986]). No experiment shows BBSE certifying under an actual shift, so 'label-shift robustness' reduces to 'declines instead of overclaiming'. Moreover, three of its four intervals are asymptotic percentile bootstraps with measured joint miscoverage 0.038 vs nominal <=0.019, so the 'finite-sample 1-delta' claim in the title/abstract does not hold for that mode as implemented.

No comparison to any external or simpler cluster-aware certifier (unanimous). The only comparator is the authors' own machinery at record granularity. Whether WSR betting on ~80 site atoms in a fixed sequence (no optional stopping over sites) is materially tighter than a one-sided cluster-level Hoeffding / empirical-Bernstein / t-based bound, a cluster bootstrap CI, or hierarchical/non-exchangeable conformal risk control (Dunn et al.; Farinhas et al.) is never shown, so the claim that the alpha frontier is a property of site count rather than the method is asserted, not demonstrated.

The motivating record-vs-site failure (E7) is weaker than framed. At the default heterogeneity s_u=0.5 the record-unit certifier grants alpha=0.05 and violates its aggregate budget in only 3.5% of draws (inside delta); the ~2delta violation appears only at s_u=2.0; at alpha=0.10 it does not violate at all (fresh-pool risk 0.081). The eICU per-site dispersion diagnostic (0.027) came in below even the synthetic default (0.055). The comparator is also run on an unjustified 2,000-record subsample of S_cal and scored against a site-weighted estimand it never claimed. The paper needs to reconcile 'record-level certificates are overconfident' with its own evidence that at realistic heterogeneity the record-level certifier stayed within budget while granting a stricter rung.

The validity evidence never stresses the certificate where it could fail: in E1 the realized fresh-pool R_M is ~0.057 against alpha=0.10 (0.048 vs 0.10 on eICU), so 0/200 exceedances mostly reflects a loose bound (information floor ~0.035 at ~80 clusters) rather than a delta-level test. There is no boundary arm with true R_M near alpha; the only failures shown are under violated assumptions.

The certified estimand is chosen for certifiability rather than clinical meaning: with M=100 and ~90% of sites over 100 records, R_M is essentially a site-equal average, and the sweep shows the record-proportional (patient-weighted) error cannot be certified at all at 208 sites. A symmetric 0-1 loss with the inherited p-hat=1/2 operating point on a ~9% mortality task, where ~77% of answered errors are false negatives, does not match the triage decision the paper motivates; sensitivity/FNR is not bounded and cost-weighted atoms are deferred.

The empirical harness is easy and narrow: the synthetic generator has d=8, linear signal on 4 features, a well-specified logistic head, and heterogeneity only via a random intercept; no non-linear head is run despite the 'model-agnostic' claim; E5 returns a null. Real-data evidence is a single cohort with 20 re-splits of one hospital population, which by the authors' admission bounds gross violation but cannot estimate a violation rate; sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV on the eICU answered set are not reported in the main text; equity is analysed by site size only, with no patient-subgroup breakdown despite abstention concentrating on sicker patients.

Presentation is dense, idiosyncratic and repetitive (unanimous Clarity 2): heavy self-characterising rhetoric ('honest', 'the system working rather than failing', 'load-bearing'), paragraph-length captions, spurious 5-6 decimal precision (e.g. ECE 0.002914, skill margin 0.003934), an abstract Results paragraph that is a wall of numbers, no formal theorem statement or algorithm box in the main text (validity argument and BBSE atom boundedness/affinity-in-rho deferred to a supplement), Figure 1 as a text schematic, and key results (BBSE certify rates across the sweep, E7 per-arm thresholds) scattered or in the SI. Related work omits group-conditional / multivalid risk-control and selective-classification disparity lines relevant to the per-site and composition discussions.
Questions: What does the betting martingale buy over a one-sided cluster-level Hoeffding / empirical-Bernstein / t-based bound or a cluster bootstrap on the same ~80 site atoms Z_c, and over hierarchical/cluster conformal risk control adapted to selective risk? Please report certify rate, coverage and the site-count frontier for at least one such comparator on the same draws.

Given that an always-negative rule already meets alpha=0.10 at ~9% prevalence and the answered-set skill margin on eICU is 0.0039, what does the certificate tell a deployer beyond the base rate? Can the framework certify a quantity that is not trivially satisfied (answered false-negative rate, cost-weighted or class-conditional atom) at 74-83 calibration clusters, and if not, what does that imply for applicability?

Is there any configuration, synthetic or real, in which the BBSE mode certifies a materially useful fraction of draws under a genuine non-null prevalence shift? Please report certify rates (not just certify-and-violate) at each intermediate target base rate in the E2 sweep, and the target-pool size / number of declared target sites needed for the rho box to reach a usable width.

Please state the BBSE-reweighted per-site atom explicitly: is it bounded in [0,1] for every rho in the box (the eICU box reaches 1.986), is the sign-deciding quantity exactly affine in rho so that testing the endpoints suffices, and given the measured 0.038 joint miscoverage what is the effective level of a label-shift-mode certificate? Will the title/abstract restrict 'finite-sample' to the exchangeable mode?

Please reconcile E7 with the motivating claim: at s_u=0.5 the record-unit certifier grants alpha=0.05 with 3.5% aggregate violation (< delta), and eICU dispersion (0.027) is below the synthetic default. Why a 2,000-record subsample of S_cal, and how do certify/violation rates change on the full record set, when scored against the record-proportional estimand the comparator actually claims, and on the eICU re-splits?

Can you add a validity stress arm where the true answered-set risk sits at or just below alpha at the deployed threshold, so that the observed exceedance rate can be compared meaningfully against delta rather than 0/200 at R_M ~ 0.057?

How do certified coverage and the reachable rung change with a stronger non-linear head (e.g. gradient boosting) on eICU, or a weaker head on the synthetic grid? The gate is claimed model-agnostic but only an L2 logistic head is ever run.

Assumption 1 requires i.i.d. calibration sites; on eICU the 74 calibration hospitals are a without-replacement subset of a fixed population of 207 from a single telehealth vendor. Does the guarantee hold in a finite-population sense, is any correction warranted, and what population does the certificate refer to for a hospital outside that network?

Please report sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of the head on the eICU answered set per re-split, a patient-subgroup breakdown of coverage and answered error (age, sex, race, admission source), the index/prediction time and feature window with handling of stays ending before it closes, and the basis for and sensitivity to the 50 record-carrying-cluster and 10-record answerable floors.
Limitations: The authors are unusually forthcoming about limitations: site-population-average scope with no per-site bound (a hospital observed at 0.29 answered error under a valid certificate), concept shift excluded, no covariate-shift mode, temporal common shocks unmodelled, symmetric loss with ~77% false negatives among answered errors and the inherited p-hat=1/2 operating point, asymptotic BBSE intervals with measured under-coverage, a single real cohort with 20 re-splits of one population, cross-hospital patients left in, git-commit pre-registration weaker than a third-party registry, and only the influence cap swept. Reviewers credit this candour.

Not adequately foregrounded as limitations of the contribution (rather than as disclosures): (i) at ~9% prevalence the only certifiable rung is met by a constant always-negative rule and the certified head barely improves on it where it answers, so the practical assurance of an alpha=0.10 certificate is thin, and no rung is reachable at all at typical consortium sizes well under 150 hospitals; (ii) the certified estimand (site-equal, symmetric 0-1) is the one that is certifiable rather than the one that maps to patient-level harm, with sensitivity/FNR unbounded; (iii) the label-shift mode is undemonstrated as a working correction; (iv) tightness relative to simpler valid cluster-level bounds is uncharacterised.

Potential negative societal impact: a 'certified' label on a gate whose answered set is enriched for survivors, and which bounds only a population average, could give deployers, procurers or regulators false assurance at the individual-hospital or patient level; abstention concentrates on the sickest patients, shifting workload and risk to clinicians via deferral, and differential deferral across demographic subgroups is unexamined on real data. The paper's disclosures mitigate but do not remove these risks; equity across hospitals is measured, not bounded.
